item.title: Just sustainability transitions in tourism
item.content:encoded:
Raymond Rastegar, Griffith University

Rami K. Isaac, Bethlehem University

Andrew Mzembe, Breda University of Applied Sciences

Lisa Ruhanen, The University of Queensland

The tourism sector stands at a critical crossroads. Amid accelerating climate crises, deepening socio-economic inequalities, biodiversity loss, enduring structural marginalisation, and regional conflicts, calls for systemic transformation have become increasingly pressing and unavoidable. While initiatives such as green transitions and the push toward net-zero have gained traction, driven by decarbonisation strategies, energy transitions, and technological innovations, these pathways are far from politically neutral. Transitions are not merely technical adjustments to energy systems or consumer behaviour; they are profoundly political processes that shape who benefits, who bears the burdens, and who has a voice or is silenced in the governance of change.

Appel publié par Journal of Sustainable Tourism. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Governance frameworks and institutional innovations for embedding justice in tourism transitions
  • Power, agency, and the role of private and public actors in driving (or resisting) transitions
  • Just sustainability transition imaginaries and realities across geographies: Global South and Global North perspectives
  • Intermediaries, social movements, labour unions and civil society in shaping justice-oriented transitions
  • Tourism workers' rights, precarity, and vulnerability in the context of transition
  • Climate change adaptation and mitigation through the lens of climate justice
  • Multispecies justice and posthuman perspectives in sustainable tourism
  • Gender justice and intersectionality in transition governance
  • Island and Indigenous tourism economies: toward self-determined transition pathways
  • Transition tourism: exploring new business models and regenerative alternatives
  • Methodologies for researching justice in sustainability transitions
  • Temporality and just transitions

item.title: Sustainable Luxury Tourism: Opportunities, Tensions, and Impacts
item.content:encoded:
Kalliopi Chatzipanagiotou, University of Glasgow

Achilleas Boukis, University of Birmingham

George Christodoulides, American University of Sharjah

Raffaele Filieri, Audencia Business School

Luxury tourism is expected to grow faster than any other industry segment. Although scholarship on luxury tourism has expanded in recent years, much of this work focuses on its economic dimensions, often overlooking its broader sustainable, social and ethical implications. The relationship between sustainability and luxury tourism has received increasing attention in recent years, yet we know little about what "sustainable luxury" actually means, given the tension between exclusivity and responsible resource use. Furthermore, while many luxury tourists express concern for sustainability, there remains limited empirical evidence on how such concerns translate into actual decision-making or on the trade-offs they are willing to accept.
